title: EFT Full Form in Banking: How It Works, Charges & Uses
summary: EFT full form in banking is Electronic Funds Transfer. Learn how it works, its types, NEFT differences, transaction charges, and international payment methods.
body_markdown:
## **What are the Different Types and Uses of EFT Payments?**


EFT payments fall into five broad types: **bank transfers, UPI payments, direct deposits, recurring payments and card payments.** Individuals and businesses use these electronic payment methods to transfer money, receive salaries, pay suppliers, settle bills and make purchases.

**Common Uses**

### **1. NEFT, RTGS and IMPS Transfers**


Individuals use NEFT and IMPS to transfer money to family members, pay rent and manage household expenses. Businesses use these systems to pay suppliers, settle vendor invoices and transfer funds to employees or other recipients. RTGS suits large-value transfers, such as large property-related payments and business settlements, as it has a minimum transaction amount of ₹2 lakh.


### **2. UPI Payments**


UPI is widely used for everyday person-to-person (P2P) and person-to-merchant (P2M) payments. Common uses include paying friends back, splitting bills, purchasing goods online, and paying merchants at physical stores through UPI IDs or QR codes. Some apps and banks also support transfers using mobile numbers or contacts, where available.


### **3. Direct Deposits and Salary Transfers**


Direct deposits allow organisations to send money electronically into beneficiaries' bank accounts. Common uses include:


-


**EFT in payroll:** Employers use electronic payment methods to deposit employees' salaries, wages, bonuses and reimbursements.


-


**Pension payments:** Government departments and other organisations transfer pension amounts directly to beneficiaries.


-


**Refunds:** Businesses and government departments credit eligible refunds to recipients' bank accounts.


-


**EFT in insurance:** Insurance companies may electronically deposit approved claim payouts into policyholders' or beneficiaries' bank accounts.


These payments may be processed individually through NEFT or in bulk through NACH credit, depending on the organisation's payment process.


### **4. Direct Debits and Recurring Payments**


Organisations use authorised recurring payment arrangements to collect money automatically from customers' accounts. Common uses include:


-


Loan instalments and EMIs


-


Insurance premiums


-


Electricity, water and other utility bills


-


Subscription fees and membership payments


In India, recurring collections may be authorised through NACH mandates, UPI AutoPay, bank standing instructions or card e-mandates, depending on the service and payment method. Customers must authorise these arrangements before recurring deductions can take place.


### **5. Card Payments**


Debit and credit cards are commonly used for online shopping, in-store purchases, travel bookings and service payments. These transactions are processed through card networks such as RuPay, Visa and Mastercard, rather than through bank-transfer systems such as NEFT or IMPS.


## **Is EFT the Same as NEFT?**


No. EFT (Electronic Funds Transfer) is a broad term for transferring money electronically between bank accounts or payment accounts. NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) is a specific payment system operated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for transferring funds between bank accounts in India.


NEFT is one of several electronic funds transfer methods in India. Others include RTGS, IMPS and UPI, each operating under its own payment system and rules.


Before NEFT was introduced in November 2005, India had earlier Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT) and Special Electronic Funds Transfer ([SEFT](https://www.rbi.org.in/commonman/english/scripts/PressReleases.aspx?Id=132) ) arrangements.


Therefore, EFT and NEFT are not interchangeable terms in modern banking. Every NEFT transaction is an electronic funds transfer, but not every electronic funds transfer is a NEFT transaction.


## **How Do NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, and UPI Differ?**


NEFT processes transfers in half-hourly batches, while RTGS processes each transaction individually in real time. IMPS and UPI allow users to transfer money instantly. NEFT and RTGS are operated by the RBI, while IMPS and UPI are managed by NPCI. Each method has different transfer limits and ways of making[payments](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/global-payment-processing) .

## **How Long Does an EFT Take, and What are the Charges?**


EFT processing time and charges depend on the[payment method](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/top-international-payment-methods-in-india-a-comprehensive-guide) , bank, transfer channel and whether the payment is domestic or international. In India, UPI and IMPS usually complete within seconds, RTGS settles transactions individually in real time, and NEFT processes transfers in half-hourly batches. International bank transfers typically take around 1-5 business days.


**Payment Method**


**Typical Processing Time**


**Charges**


NEFT


Half-hourly batches; beneficiary credit generally within two hours of batch settlement


Free for savings account holders using internet or mobile banking; other channels may attract charges


RTGS


Real-time, transaction-by-transaction


No charge for inward transfers; outward charges depend on the bank and channel, within RBI limits


IMPS


Usually immediate

Usually within seconds

**Note:** India's major retail payment systems operate 24×7, including on holidays. Systems such as US ACH and UK Bacs generally follow business-day schedules and cut-off times.


**UPI MDR update:** NPCI has deferred the proposed MDR on select merchant UPI transactions until after Diwali, with a new implementation date to be notified separately. The MDR is payable by merchants, not consumers, and does not apply to P2P payments. Check NPCI's latest announcements for the current implementation status.


### **What Costs Can Add Up on a Transfer?**


Domestic transfers may involve:


-


**Bank charges:** Fees for certain transfer methods, account types, or channels.


-


**Service fees and taxes:** Provider fees and applicable GST on eligible services.


International transfers may also involve:


-


**Intermediary bank charges:** Fees deducted by correspondent banks.


-


**Foreign exchange markup:** An additional cost when converting currencies.


-


**Receiving bank fees:** Charges imposed by the beneficiary's bank.


Actual charges depend on the bank, provider, and payment route. Check the latest fee schedule before transferring money.


The next section explains how domestic and international EFT payments differ, including the additional steps and costs involved in cross-border transfers.


## **Is EFT Safe, and What Happens If It Fails or Goes to the Wrong Account?**


Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT) is generally safe because banks and payment providers use authentication and security measures to protect transactions. However, users must verify recipient details, protect their banking credentials, and report suspicious or incorrect transactions immediately.


Follow these precautions when making an electronic funds transfer:


-


**Use official channels:** Make payments through your bank's official website or mobile app.


-


**Verify recipient details:** Check the beneficiary's name, account number,[IFSC](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/ifsc-vs-swift-code-essentials-for-international-payments) or UPI ID before confirming the payment.


-


**Protect your credentials:** Never share your OTP, UPI PIN, password, or other confidential banking credentials. You do not need to enter a UPI PIN to receive money.


-


**Check payment requests:** Do not approve unexpected UPI collect requests or payment authorisations.


-


**Save transaction records:** Keep the transaction reference number or UTR for future reference.


-


**Report suspicious activity:** Contact your bank immediately if you notice an unauthorised transaction or suspect your credentials have been compromised. If you suspect online financial fraud, call the national cybercrime helpline at 1930 or report it at cybercrime.gov.in.


### **What Should You Do If an EFT Fails?**


A failed EFT occurs when money is debited from the sender's account, but the beneficiary does not receive it. For eligible domestic IMPS and UPI fund transfers, the amount must generally be reversed by **T+1 day** . For eligible UPI merchant payments where the sender is debited but the merchant does not receive transaction confirmation, the reversal must generally happen within T+5 days. These are prescribed outer timelines under RBI rules.


If your payment fails, follow these steps:


1.


**Check the transaction status:** Open your bank app or payment platform to confirm whether the payment is pending, failed, or successful.


2.


**Save the transaction details:** Note the transaction reference number or UTR, date, amount, and beneficiary details.


3.


**Contact your bank:** Raise a complaint with your bank if the amount has been debited but not credited to the beneficiary. Keep the complaint acknowledgement for follow-up.


4.


**Check the reversal:** Ask the bank when the amount should be credited back to your account.


**RBI compensation rule:** If an eligible failed transaction is not reversed within the prescribed timeline, the responsible bank or payment system **participant must pay compensation of ₹100 per day of delay.** This amount must be credited to the customer's account automatically, without requiring a separate complaint or claim. The applicable **T+1 or T+5 timeline** depends on the transaction type.


### **What Should You Do If You Transfer Money to the Wrong Account?**


A successful transfer to the wrong account differs from a failed transaction. The payment has reached the account specified in the transfer instruction, so an automatic reversal under the failed-transaction timelines does not apply.


If you send money to the wrong account:


1.


**Contact your bank immediately:** Report the incorrect transfer and request help recovering the funds.


2.


**Share the transaction details:** Provide the UTR or transaction reference number, amount, date, and incorrect beneficiary details.


3.


**Request a recovery process:** Your bank may contact the recipient's bank and seek the recipient's consent to return the money.


4.


**Follow up on the complaint:** Keep the complaint reference number and check the recovery status with your bank.


Recovery is not guaranteed, particularly if the recipient does not agree to return the money. RTGS settlements are final and irrevocable, so an incorrect RTGS transfer cannot simply be cancelled.


### **Can an EFT Payment Be Cancelled or Reversed?**


Whether an electronic payment can be stopped or recovered depends on its payment method and transaction status.


**Payment Type**


**Can It Be Stopped or Reversed?**


Scheduled payments or standing instructions


May be cancelled before execution, subject to bank rules and cut-off times.


Direct debits or mandates


You can generally stop future collections by revoking the mandate within the applicable timeline. A processed debit is not automatically reversed.


NEFT


A processed transfer generally cannot be unilaterally cancelled. Contact the bank immediately if sent incorrectly.


RTGS


Settlement is final and irrevocable. Recovery of an incorrect transfer is not guaranteed.


IMPS and UPI


Successful transfers generally cannot be cancelled after processing. If money is sent to the wrong recipient, contact the bank immediately to request recovery.


Card payments


Eligible disputed transactions may be raised with the card issuer through a dispute or chargeback process, subject to applicable rules.


If your bank does not resolve the complaint:


-


First approach your bank or payment provider and raise a formal complaint.


-


You can approach the RBI Ombudsman if you receive an unsatisfactory response, or if the bank does not respond within 30 days or the longer timeline specified by RBI, NPCI or the card network, where applicable.


-


If you receive no response, file the Ombudsman complaint within 90 days after the applicable response timeline expires. If you are dissatisfied with the bank's reply, file it within 90 days of the bank's last communication.


The complaint must meet the eligibility requirements of the Reserve Bank–Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026. You can file eligible complaints through the RBI Complaint Management System.


## **How are Domestic and International EFT Payments Different?**


Domestic and international EFT payments both transfer money electronically, but they differ in payment routes, currencies, participating financial institutions, processing times, costs and regulatory requirements. Domestic transfers take place within one country, while international transfers move money across national borders and may involve[foreign exchange conversion](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/understanding-currency-conversion-for-international-payments) and[intermediary banks](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/what-are-intermediary-banks) .


**Feature**


**Domestic EFT**


**International EFT**


Geography

Currency


Usually the domestic currency

Payment routes

Processing time


Depends on the domestic payment system

Costs


May include domestic bank or service charges

Compliance

Involves applicable cross-border, KYC, AML and foreign exchange requirements


In India, domestic EFT payments use systems such as NEFT, RTGS, IMPS and UPI. International EFT payments may use the SWIFT network and correspondent banking arrangements or other cross-border payment routes. SWIFT is a financial messaging network that enables banks and other financial institutions to exchange payment instructions. It is not a bank, does not hold customer funds and does not itself transfer money between accounts. The actual transfer and settlement take place through participating financial institutions.


International transfers may also involve foreign exchange conversion, intermediary bank charges and additional compliance checks. Banks and payment providers may verify the sender, recipient, source of funds and purpose of payment to meet applicable KYC, AML and foreign exchange requirements. Additional documents may be required depending on the transaction.


The exact payment route, processing time, charges and documentation depend on the countries, currencies, banks and payment method involved. The next section explains how Indian businesses can receive international payments electronically.


## **How Can Indian Businesses Receive International Payments Electronically?**


Indian freelancers, agencies, exporters and other businesses can[receive international payments](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/receive-international-payments-in-india-in-2026) through bank transfers or cross-border payment platforms. The right method depends on the available payment routes, supported currencies, fees and documentation requirements.


**Two common receiving methods are:**


1.


**International bank transfers:** Overseas clients send money to an Indian bank account through an international wire transfer, which may involve SWIFT messaging and correspondent banks.


2.


**Local receiving accounts:** Payment platforms provide eligible users with local bank details in supported foreign markets. Clients can use these details to pay through local banking systems, such as ACH in the US.


### **Global Accounts vs International SWIFT Accounts**


Global Accounts provide local receiving details in supported markets, while an International SWIFT Account supports incoming international wire transfers. These are different payment routes.

Available routes, currencies, eligibility, fees and documentation depend on the payment provider and its banking arrangements.


Before choosing a route, check the transaction fee, foreign exchange markup, intermediary bank charges and applicable taxes. International payments may also require supporting documents.[FIRA (Foreign Inward Remittance Advice)](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/what-is-fira-its-importance-for-freelancers-in-india) records an inward foreign remittance and serves as evidence of the payment. A purpose code classifies the reason for receiving the payment for regulatory reporting. Requirements depend on the transaction and applicable regulations.

## **Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) About EFT Full Form**


### **1. What is the full form of EFT in banking?**


EFT stands for Electronic Funds Transfer. It refers to the electronic movement of money between bank accounts or payment accounts without using cash or paper-based payment instruments. In India, NEFT, RTGS, IMPS and UPI are common methods of electronic funds transfer.


### **2. What does EFT mean on a bank statement?**


EFT on a bank statement generally indicates an electronic funds transfer, meaning money was sent or received electronically. However, the label alone may not identify the exact payment method. Check the transaction description, reference number, or contact your bank to confirm the transaction type.


### **3. Is EFT the same as NEFT?**


No. EFT (Electronic Funds Transfer) is a broad term for electronic money transfers, while NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) is a specific bank transfer system operated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). NEFT is one type of electronic funds transfer, alongside RTGS, IMPS and UPI.


### **4. Can EFT be used for international money transfers?**


Yes. Electronic funds transfers can be used for international payments through cross-border bank transfer routes and payment providers. These transfers may involve SWIFT messaging, correspondent banks or local receiving accounts in supported countries. Processing time, fees, currency conversion and documentation depend on the payment route and provider.


### **5. What is the difference between EFT and ETF?**


EFT stands for Electronic Funds Transfer, which means moving money electronically between accounts. ETF stands for Exchange-Traded Fund, an investment fund whose units are traded on a stock exchange, much like shares. EFT is a payment process, while ETF is an investment product.
